lines.line: As a kid, Adolf wasn't very social. He found it hard to connect.
When he went to a summer camp...
Danny said: "OK, you can join. You just have to share."
And then he said: "My camp, mine <<ˈ|k|ɑː|m|p|f>>. Potato, <<p|ə|ˈ|t|ɑː|t|oʊ>>, right?"
He never got it. He had issues with possessives.
Honestly, he was a bit possessive.
Later we realised it wasn't only his English. He was really struggling.
Which is why he called his book... Mein <<ˈ|k|ɑː|m|p|f>>.

transcript.heard: As a kid, Adolf wasn't very social. He found it hard to connect. When he went to a summer camp, Danny said, welcome to my camp. Hitler answered, it is mine. Danny said, okay, you can join. You just have to share. Hitler answered, this camp is mine. And then he said, my camp, Mein Kampf. Potato potato, right? He never got it. He had issues with possessives. Also with possessions. Honestly, he was a bit possessive. He was a bit possessed. Later we realized it wasn't only his English, he was really struggling. Which is why he called his book, Mein Kampf. My struggle. The struggle was real, maybe because.
